opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, the biggest challenge was figuring out what to leave out. When you work in AI research every day, you're surrounded by jargon and by all these fascinating technical details, and it's very tempting to want to explain everything. But the format of the series is deliberately short and accessible, so I had to keep asking myself: what does a curious, intelligent person who isn't in the field actually need to understand to make sense of what's happening right now?

So I tried to start from the questions people actually ask me. When I talk to friends, family, or people at dinner parties, they want to know things like: Is this thing actually intelligent? Is it going to take my job? Can I trust what it tells me? Where is this all heading? I organized the ideas around those kinds of concerns rather than around how a textbook would structure the field.

Another thing I cared about was being honest about uncertainty. There's a lot of hype on one side and a lot of doom on the other, and I think a general audience deserves a more grounded picture: here's what these systems can genuinely do, here's where they still fall short, and here's what even the experts don't know yet. I also wanted to convey some of the excitement I feel, particularly around open-endedness and the idea of systems that keep learning and discovering new things, because that's what got me into research in the first place.

And finally, I tried to use concrete examples and analogies wherever possible. Abstract explanations of neural networks don't stick, but a good example of a model doing something surprising, or failing in an interesting way, really helps people build intuition. So it was a bit like translating, keeping the substance accurate while making it feel approachable.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The honest answer is that it was harder than I expected, and in a way that surprised me.

When you work in research, you're used to writing for people who share your vocabulary. You can say "gradient descent" or "reinforcement learning" and move on. With this book, the brief was essentially: ten things, short chapters, a reader who is curious but has no technical background and maybe only an hour or two on a train. So the first thing I had to do was let go of the idea that I was going to explain how any of this actually works at a mechanistic level. That's not what the reader needs, and frankly it's not what would help them.

What I kept coming back to was: what does someone actually need to know to think clearly about AI? Not to build it, but to read a headline about it and not be either terrified or dismissive. So the ten things ended up being more like ten ideas or framings than ten facts. Things like: these systems learn from data rather than being programmed rule by rule, and almost everything that's strange or surprising about them follows from that. Or that intelligence isn't one thing, so it's perfectly possible for a system to be superhuman at one task and hopeless at a neighbouring one, and that shouldn't be confusing once you have the right mental model.

The other thing I tried to do was be honest about uncertainty. There's a temptation when writing for a general audience to sound more confident than you are, because confidence reads well. But the field genuinely doesn't know a lot of things, including some quite fundamental ones, and I think readers can handle that. In some ways it's more interesting to say "here is what we know, here is what we're arguing about, and here is why the argument matters" than to hand down a verdict.

And then there was a lot of just cutting. My first drafts were full of caveats and asides, the kind of thing you put in a paper to pre-empt reviewer two. Almost all of that had to go. I had friends outside the field read it and tell me where they got lost, and the answer was usually that I'd tried to be too precise rather than too simple. Open-endedness was something I wanted to get in, because it's close to my own work and I think it's underappreciated, but even there I had to find a way to talk about it through examples rather than definitions.

So I'd say the approach was: pick the ideas that change how someone sees the field, be honest about what's unresolved, and be ruthless about anything that only exists to make me feel safe as a researcher.

astra-6.text:
I think the challenge is deciding what to leave out. AI is a very broad field, and for a general audience you want to give people a useful way to think about it without assuming a background in mathematics or computer science.

So the approach is to start with the intuition: what does it mean for a machine to learn from examples? How is that different from someone explicitly programming every rule? You can get quite far with those questions before you need technical terminology.

And then you have to balance the excitement with the limitations. A system can do something very impressive and still make surprisingly basic mistakes. I wanted to help readers hold both of those ideas at once—to appreciate the possibilities while being able to ask sensible questions about what these systems can actually do.

sol-6.1.text:
The challenge was deciding what to leave out. AI is such a broad field, and you can very quickly get drawn into technical details. I wanted to give readers an intuition for how these systems work without assuming a background in mathematics or computer science.

So I focused on the ideas behind the technology: what it means for a machine to learn from data, why that can be useful, and where it can go wrong. Concrete examples help make those ideas accessible. And I wanted to convey both the excitement and the limitations, so that readers could come away better equipped to assess the claims they hear about AI.
